mustMemorise: Vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta

The left ventricle has the thickest wall: it pumps to the whole body
Valves prevent backflow, so blood flows one way only
Coronary vessels supply the heart muscle itself
Liver: hepatic artery in, hepatic vein out, hepatic portal vein from the intestine. Kidney: renal artery in, renal vein out
Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate (given to you whenever a question needs it)
Regular exercise strengthens the heart muscle and increases cardiac output at rest

sheet.howExamined: B2, 1 hour 15 minutes: 70 marks at Foundation, 80 at Higher, calculator allowed. The heart usually opens the paper, as a labelled section or a circulation diagram with organs and vessels to name at [1] each, an arrow for the direction of flow, and a [2] explanation of wall thickness. Exercise comes in as a pulse graph with a reading and a calculation. The accept lists are tight: 'aorta' not 'main artery', 'capillary' not 'small vein', and a valve question wants one valve labelled, not all of them.
traps: Giving the aorta's name wrongly — examiners saw a complete range of other vessels (Summer 2024 B2 Foundation Q1)

noteBlocks.md: The heart is a muscular pump with four chambers. The two upper chambers, the **atria**, receive blood from the veins; the two lower ones, the **ventricles**, contract and pump it out. The **right** side sends blood to the lungs, the **left** side round the body, and a wall of muscle, the **septum**, keeps the two sides apart.

noteBlocks.title: Why the left wall is the thickest
noteBlocks.md: The left ventricle pumps blood all the way round the body, so it must build a higher pressure than the right ventricle, which pumps only as far as the nearby lungs. More muscle makes more pressure.

noteBlocks.alt: A dissected sheep heart held in a hand and cut across below the atria, so both ventricles are open. On the left of the cut face a thick ring of dark muscle surrounds a small round cavity; on the right a much thinner wall surrounds a wide crescent-shaped cavity.
noteBlocks.caption: A real sheep heart cut across: the round, thick-walled left ventricle beside the thin crescent of the right.
noteBlocks.prompt: Which ventricle is which in this photograph, and what does the difference in wall thickness tell you about where each one has to pump?

noteBlocks.stem: A heart is drawn from the front. Chamber X is a lower chamber on the right-hand side of the page, and its wall is the thickest in the heart. Explain how you can tell that X is (a) a ventricle and (b) the left ventricle. [2]

steps.working: (a) It is one of the two lower chambers.
steps.decision: The ventricles are the lower, larger chambers; the atria sit above them.

steps.working: (b) Its wall is thicker than the other ventricle's, and the right of the page is the person's left.
steps.decision: The thickest wall belongs to the chamber that pumps blood round the whole body.

noteBlocks.prompt: A heart is drawn from the front. Chamber M is an upper chamber on the right-hand side of the page. Which chamber is it?
noteBlocks.explain: Turn the diagram to face you, as the worked answer did: the right of the page is the person's left side, and an upper chamber is an atrium. So M is the left atrium.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because M is on the right of the page, but the heart faces you, so the right of the page is the person's left.
It tempts because the left ventricle is the chamber asked about most, but ventricles are the lower chambers and M is an upper one.

twin.prompt: Chamber N is a lower chamber on the left-hand side of the page, with a thinner wall than the other lower chamber. Which chamber is it?
twin.explain: The left of the page is the person's right, and a lower chamber is a ventricle. The thinner wall fits: the right ventricle pumps only to the lungs.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because N is on the left of the page, but the page's left is the person's right, and the left ventricle has the thicker wall.
It tempts because N is on the person's right, but the atria are the upper chambers and N is a lower one.

noteBlocks.md: Every vessel is named by its direction. An **artery** carries blood **away** from the heart; a **vein** carries it **towards** the heart. What the blood carries plays no part in the name.

So the lung vessels are the two that surprise. The **pulmonary artery** carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs (there are two, one to each lung), and the **pulmonary vein** brings oxygenated blood back to the left atrium. The **aorta** leaves the left ventricle for the body; the **vena cava** brings blood back to the right atrium.

noteBlocks.stem: Explain why the pulmonary artery is an artery, even though the blood inside it is deoxygenated. [2]

steps.working: It carries blood away from the heart, from the right ventricle to the lungs.
steps.decision: Start from where the vessel runs: out of the heart.

steps.working: A vessel is named by the direction of flow, not by its blood: away from the heart makes it an artery.
steps.decision: Then the rule itself, which is what the second mark is for.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which vessel carries oxygenated blood towards the heart?
noteBlocks.explain: Towards the heart makes it a vein, as the worked answer's rule said, and oxygenated blood comes from the lungs. The vein bringing it back from the lungs is the pulmonary vein.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because arteries are thought of as the oxygen carriers, but this one runs away from the heart, with deoxygenated blood.
It tempts because it does flow towards the heart, but its blood comes from the body and is deoxygenated.

twin.prompt: Which vessel carries oxygenated blood away from the heart?
twin.explain: Away from the heart makes it an artery, and oxygenated blood leaves from the left ventricle: the aorta. The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood, and the pulmonary vein flows towards the heart.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because it is the other artery leaving the heart, but it carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs.
It tempts because it carries oxygenated blood, but it flows towards the heart, so it is a vein.

noteBlocks.md: Follow one drop of blood from the body and back: **vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta**. On each side it enters an atrium, passes through a valve into the ventricle below, and leaves in an artery.
One full circuit of the body passes through the heart **twice**, once for each loop: a **double circulation**. Blood coming back from the lungs is pumped again before it sets off round the body.

noteBlocks.stem:
Complete the route by naming the chamber or vessel in each numbered box. [4]
body → 1 → right atrium → 2 → pulmonary artery → lungs → 3 → left atrium → 4 → aorta

steps.decision: The vein that brings blood back from the body into the right atrium.
From an atrium, blood passes through a valve into the ventricle on the same side.
Back from the lungs towards the heart, so a vein.
The left atrium passes blood down to the left ventricle, which pumps it into the aorta.

noteBlocks.title: GCSE Biology Revision "The Heart and Circulation"
noteBlocks.why: A second pass over the chambers and the route, now that you have worked it through yourself.

noteBlocks.prompt: On one complete circuit of the body, how many times does the blood pass through the heart?
noteBlocks.explain: Twice, as the worked route showed: once through the right side on the way to the lungs, once through the left side on the way to the body. That is what double circulation means.

twin.prompt: How many chambers of the heart does blood pass through between leaving the vena cava and entering the aorta?
twin.explain: The right atrium and the right ventricle, then, after the lungs, the left atrium and the left ventricle: four.

noteBlocks.text: Valves and the heart's own supply

noteBlocks.md: **Valves** keep the blood moving one way. One sits between each atrium and its ventricle, and one at the base of each artery leaving the heart, the aorta and the pulmonary artery. When the ventricles relax, the valves at the base of the arteries shut, so blood cannot fall back into the heart.

The heart muscle needs its own oxygen and glucose. The **coronary arteries** branch from the aorta and run over the outside of the heart; **coronary veins** drain it. If a coronary artery is blocked, the muscle beyond it is starved of oxygen.

noteBlocks.stem: When the ventricles relax, which valves shut, and what does their shutting prevent? [2]

steps.working: The valves at the base of the aorta and the pulmonary artery shut.
steps.decision: Name the valves first: they sit at the start of the two arteries leaving the heart.

steps.working: They stop the blood in those arteries flowing back into the ventricles, so it moves one way.
steps.decision: Then the job: stopping backflow is the idea the mark is for.

noteBlocks.prompt: The valve between the left atrium and the left ventricle does not close properly. When the left ventricle contracts, where does some blood leak?
noteBlocks.explain: Locate the valve as the worked answer did: this one sits between the left atrium and the left ventricle. When the ventricle squeezes, blood meant for the aorta can also be pushed back through the gap into the left atrium.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because the ventricles sit side by side, but the septum keeps the two sides apart, whatever the valves do.
It tempts because the vena cava brings blood into the heart, but it joins the right atrium, on the other side of the septum.

twin.prompt: The valve at the base of the pulmonary artery does not close properly. When the right ventricle relaxes, where does some blood flow?
twin.explain: That valve should shut as the ventricle relaxes. If it cannot, blood in the pulmonary artery falls back into the right ventricle.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because the pulmonary artery leads to the lungs, but a leaking valve lets blood go backwards, not faster forwards.
It tempts because the ventricles lie side by side, but the septum keeps the two sides apart.

noteBlocks.text: Every organ has its own pair

noteBlocks.md: Every organ has an artery bringing blood **in** and a vein taking it **out**, named after the organ: **renal** for the kidney, **hepatic** for the liver, **pulmonary** for the lungs, **mesenteric** for the intestine. The arteries branch from the aorta; the veins lead back to the vena cava.
One vessel breaks the pattern. The intestine's veins do not lead back to the vena cava: they join the **hepatic portal vein**, which carries blood rich in digested food straight to the liver.

noteBlocks.stem: For each vessel, name the organ it is joined to and say whether its blood flows into that organ or out of it. (a) the mesenteric artery (b) the hepatic vein (c) the pulmonary vein [3]

steps.decision: An artery brings blood in, and mesenteric means the intestine.
A vein takes blood out, and hepatic means the liver.

steps.working: (c) Out of the lungs, back to the heart.
steps.decision: Pulmonary means the lungs; a vein leaves the organ for the heart.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which vessel takes blood out of the kidneys?
noteBlocks.explain: Out of an organ means a vein, as the worked answer read each name, and renal means the kidney. So blood leaves the kidneys in the renal vein.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because renal is the right organ, but an artery brings blood into the kidney.
It tempts because it is a vein leaving an organ, but hepatic means the liver.

twin.prompt: Which vessel brings oxygenated blood to the liver?
twin.explain: Into an organ, with oxygenated blood from the aorta, means the artery: the hepatic artery. The hepatic portal vein brings blood from the intestine, and the hepatic vein takes blood away.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because it also carries blood into the liver, but its blood comes from the intestine and has given up oxygen there.
It tempts because hepatic is the right organ, but the hepatic vein takes blood out of the liver.

noteBlocks.md: During exercise the muscles contract more, so they respire faster to release more energy. They need oxygen and glucose delivered faster, and their extra carbon dioxide taken away, so the heart beats faster and the **pulse rate** rises. It stays raised for a while after the exercise stops.
The pulse is each heartbeat felt in an artery near the skin, at the wrist or the neck, so counting it measures the heart rate.

noteBlocks.stem: Describe how a student should measure her resting pulse rate. [3]

steps.working: Sit still for a few minutes first, so the pulse settles at its resting rate.
steps.decision: Resting means resting: a pulse taken straight after moving is still raised.

steps.working: Press two fingers, not a thumb, on the artery at the wrist and count the beats for 15 seconds, then multiply by 4.
steps.decision: A thumb has a pulse of its own; 15 seconds times 4 gives beats per minute.

steps.working: Repeat twice more and take the mean.
steps.decision: Repeats smooth out a miscount.

noteBlocks.prompt: A student counts 21 beats at her wrist in 15 seconds. What is her pulse rate, in beats per minute?
noteBlocks.explain: Scale 15 seconds up to a minute, as step 2 of the worked answer did: 21 × 4 = 84 beats per minute.

twin.prompt: He counts 19 beats in 15 seconds. What is his pulse rate, in beats per minute?

noteBlocks.text: Cardiac output, and what training does

noteBlocks.md: **Cardiac output** is the volume of blood the heart pumps in one minute: **cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate**, where the stroke volume is the volume pumped out in one beat. Multiply, because one stroke volume leaves the heart on every beat.

Regular exercise **strengthens the heart muscle**, so it pumps more blood in each beat and needs fewer beats at rest: a fit person's resting pulse is lower. The specification's words for the benefit are **increased cardiac output when at rest**; CCEA's 2019 scheme also accepted 'pumps more blood per beat'.

noteBlocks.stem:
At rest, a student's stroke volume is 60 cm³ and her heart rate is 80 beats per minute.
(a) Calculate her cardiac output. [2]
(b) During a run her cardiac output rises to 12 000 cm³ per minute. Calculate the percentage increase. [3]

steps.decision: Multiply: one stroke volume on every beat, and 80 beats in a minute.
Find the increase before any percentage.
Divide by the value she started from, the resting output.

noteBlocks.prompt: A man's stroke volume is 90 cm³ and his heart rate is 58 beats per minute. What is his cardiac output, in cm³ per minute?
noteBlocks.explain: Multiply, as the worked answer did at rest: 90 × 58 = 5220 cm³ per minute. Adding the two numbers gives nothing meaningful: they are different kinds of quantity.

twin.prompt: A cyclist's stroke volume is 85 cm³ and his heart rate is 62 beats a minute. Work out his cardiac output in cm³ per minute.

noteBlocks.md: **Label a valve, or name an organ.** When a question says label *a* valve, draw one line to one valve: in Summer 2024 a few labelled every valve. On a body plan, match each organ to its vessels: in Summer 2025 brain and intestine were the commonest wrong answers where the lungs and a kidney were meant.

**Who is fittest?** With three people, compare each measure with both of the others: 'the lowest of the three', never just 'low'. Remember the resting rate: on a Unit 1 breathing graph in March 2026, fewer candidates gave the lower resting rate as evidence of fitness.

steps.decision: A fitter heart pumps more per beat, so it needs fewer beats at rest; state it against both others.

steps.decision: The same reason holds while exercising: fewer beats move the blood the muscles need.

items.stem: Before we start, three things from the last topic. Which vessel carries blood AWAY from the heart?

options.feedback: An artery. That definition is about direction, not about oxygen — which matters more than you would think in this topic.
Veins carry blood back towards the heart. Arteries carry it away.
Capillaries are the tiny exchange vessels between the two.
That is the trap this topic is built on. Artery and vein are defined by direction, not by the blood they carry.

items.stem: What do the valves in a vein do?

options.feedback: They prevent backflow. The valves in the heart do exactly the same job.
A valve has no muscle: it can only open or shut. The pumping is done by the heart and by the muscles around the vein.
Filtering blood is the kidney's job.

options.text: They control how much oxygen the blood carries
options.feedback: Oxygen is picked up in the lungs and carried by haemoglobin, not controlled by valves.

items.stem: Where does blood exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide with the body's tissues?

options.feedback: Capillaries: wall one cell thick and permeable, so the diffusion distance is tiny.
An artery's wall is far too thick for anything to diffuse across.
By the time blood reaches a vein the exchange has already happened.
The heart is a pump. Exchange happens out in the tissues.

items.stem: Which chamber of the heart pumps blood into the aorta?
items.skill: Name the chambers and what leaves them

options.feedback: The left ventricle, with the thickest wall, because the aorta feeds the whole body.
The right ventricle pumps into the pulmonary artery, which goes only as far as the lungs.
An atrium receives blood and passes it down to the ventricle below it. Ventricles do the pumping out.
The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the vena cava.

items.stem: Which vessel carries deoxygenated blood away from the heart?

options.feedback: The odd one out: an artery carrying deoxygenated blood, because 'artery' means away from the heart.
The pulmonary vein brings oxygenated blood back from the lungs.
The vena cava does carry deoxygenated blood, but towards the heart, not away from it.
The aorta carries oxygenated blood away from the heart to the body.

items.stem: Why is the wall of the left ventricle thicker than the wall of the right ventricle?

options.text: It has to pump blood all the way round the body, not just to the lungs
options.feedback: Further to pump means more pressure needed, which means more muscle.

options.text: It holds more blood than the right ventricle
options.feedback: Both ventricles push out about the same volume each beat — they have to, or blood would pile up on one side.

options.text: It receives blood from the lungs, which is at higher pressure
options.feedback: Blood arriving from the lungs is at low pressure. The thick wall is about what the ventricle has to do next.

options.text: It contains the valves, which need thicker muscle around them
options.feedback: Both sides have valves, and valves are flaps of tissue, not muscle.

items.stem: Which vessel carries blood containing digested food from the intestine to the liver?
items.skill: Name the vessels of the organs

options.feedback: The hepatic portal vein: the one vessel that runs from one organ's capillaries straight to another's.
The hepatic artery brings oxygenated blood to the liver from the aorta.
The hepatic vein takes blood away from the liver, back towards the vena cava.
Renal means kidney. Hepatic means liver.

items.stem: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate. A person's stroke volume is 70 cm³ and her heart rate is 68 beats per minute. What is her cardiac output?

options.feedback: 70 × 68: one stroke volume for every beat, and that many beats a minute.
The two numbers have been added. A volume and a rate cannot be added; multiplying them gives a volume per minute.
Dividing gives the volume per beat per beat, which is not a quantity. Multiply.
That is the volume of a single beat. Cardiac output is what the heart pumps in a whole minute.

items.stem: What happens to the circulatory system after months of regular exercise?
items.skill: Recall the effects of regular exercise

options.text: The heart muscle is strengthened and cardiac output at rest increases
options.feedback: Those are the specification's own two effects. A stronger heart pushes out more per beat, so it can beat more slowly.

options.text: The heart muscle is strengthened and cardiac output at rest decreases
options.feedback: A stronger heart pumps more blood in each beat, so it can beat more slowly at rest. The specification calls the benefit an increased cardiac output when at rest.
The number of valves never changes: four, for life.

options.text: The blood carries more carbon dioxide
options.feedback: Training changes the pump, not the composition of the blood being pumped.

parts.stem: Use the graph to work out how long her pulse took to return to its resting rate after she stopped running.

scheme.for: 5 minutes (from the peak at 6 minutes to the resting rate again)

hints: Find the peak, then find where the line settles back.
parts.workedSolution: Her pulse peaked at 6 minutes and was back to 68 beats per minute at 11 minutes, so recovery took 5 minutes.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the time at which her pulse was back to normal, read straight off the axis. The question asks how long recovery took, so subtract the time she stopped running.

parts.stem: During the run her stroke volume was 110 cm³ and her pulse was 153 beats per minute. Calculate her cardiac output, in cm³ per minute.
hints: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate.
parts.workedSolution: 110 × 153 = 16830 cm³ per minute, which is 16.83 dm³ every minute.

commonErrors.feedback: The two numbers have been added. Multiply: one stroke volume leaves the heart on every beat.

parts.stem: Explain why her cardiac output rises so much during the run.

accepted: her muscles are respiring faster, so they need more oxygen and glucose and produce more carbon dioxide, and a greater cardiac output delivers the oxygen and removes the carbon dioxide more quickly

scheme.for: her muscles are respiring faster to release more energy
so they need oxygen and glucose delivered more quickly
and the carbon dioxide they produce has to be removed more quickly

hints: Start with what the muscles are doing, then say what they need and what they make.
parts.workedSolution: Her leg muscles are respiring much faster during the run, to release the energy she needs for contraction. Respiring faster means they need oxygen and glucose delivered more quickly, and they produce carbon dioxide more quickly too. A greater cardiac output moves more blood through the muscles every minute, so it delivers the oxygen and glucose and carries the carbon dioxide away.

commonErrors.feedback: Respiration releases energy from glucose; it does not make it. CCEA's schemes are strict about that wording.

context.setting: One drop of blood followed all the way round the body

parts.stem:
Follow one drop of blood from the moment it returns to the heart from the body until it leaves for the body again.
Describe its route, naming the chambers and vessels it passes through, and explain why the blood passes through the heart twice on each circuit.
The quality of your written communication is marked here too, including your use of specialist scientific terms.

bands.descriptor: Five or six of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist terms used widely and accurately; everything set out in a clear and sensible order; spelling, punctuation and grammar make the meaning clear throughout.

Three or four of the indicative points; some specialist vocabulary; an order you can follow, though it is not held right through; spelling, punctuation and grammar are competent enough for the meaning to be clear.
One or two of the indicative points; little specialist vocabulary; ideas in an order that is hard to follow; spelling, punctuation and grammar may leave what you meant unclear.

indicativeContent.point: deoxygenated blood returns from the body in the vena cava and enters the right atrium
it passes into the right ventricle, through a valve that prevents backflow
the right ventricle pumps it out through the pulmonary artery to the lungs
in the lungs it picks up oxygen and becomes oxygenated
it returns in the pulmonary vein to the left atrium, then into the left ventricle
the left ventricle pumps it out through the aorta to the body; its wall is thickest because it pumps the whole way round
passing through the heart twice restores the pressure after the lungs, so the blood reaches the whole body quickly

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: A route with the pulmonary artery and pulmonary vein swapped cannot reach Band A, because the error runs through the whole answer. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: Nine names in order: vena cava, right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary artery, lungs, pulmonary vein, left atrium, left ventricle, aorta.
The last point is the one most answers miss: why twice, and what the second pass does to the pressure.
parts.workedSolution: Deoxygenated blood returns from the body in the vena cava and enters the right atrium. It passes down into the right ventricle through a valve, which shuts to prevent backflow when the ventricle contracts. The right ventricle pumps the blood out through the pulmonary artery to the lungs, where it picks up oxygen and becomes oxygenated. It returns to the heart in the pulmonary vein, entering the left atrium, and passes down into the left ventricle. The left ventricle has the thickest wall, because it pumps the blood all the way round the body, out through the aorta. The blood passes through the heart twice on each circuit because the trip through the tiny capillaries of the lungs leaves it at low pressure; returning to the heart restores that pressure, so the blood can be pushed quickly to every organ.

commonErrors.feedback: The vessel leaving the right ventricle is the pulmonary artery: an artery carries blood away from the heart, whatever blood it holds. Swapping them runs an error through the whole route.

findTheMistake.stem:
Daire is asked: 'Describe the route of blood from the right ventricle to the left ventricle. [3]'
His answer:
studentWorking: The right ventricle pumps blood into the pulmonary vein.
That vessel carries it to the lungs, where it picks up oxygen.
It comes back to the left atrium, and then into the left ventricle.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The two pulmonary vessels have been swapped. A vessel is an artery because it carries blood AWAY from the heart, not because of the blood inside it — so the vessel leaving the right ventricle is the pulmonary artery, even though the blood in it is deoxygenated. The one bringing blood back from the lungs is the pulmonary vein.
correction: The right ventricle pumps blood into the pulmonary artery.
That vessel carries it to the lungs, where it picks up oxygen.
It comes back in the pulmonary vein to the left atrium, and then into the left ventricle.
findTheMistake.feedback: One mark of the three: the lungs and the oxygen are right, and so is the chamber order. The two vessel marks go together, because one swap makes both names wrong. Fix it with the rule rather than the picture: artery means away, vein means towards, and the pulmonary pair is the exception that proves it.

findTheMistake.stem:
Niamh is asked: 'Her resting pulse rate was 64 beats per minute and it rose to 112 during exercise. Calculate the percentage increase. [3]'
Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 is right. Line 2 turns the fraction upside down: the increase is divided by the value she started from, 48 ÷ 64, not the other way round, and line 3 carries the slip on.
findTheMistake.feedback: One mark of three, for the increase. A quick check catches it: 133.3% would mean her pulse more than doubled, and 112 is less than twice 64.

prompts.answer: They prevent backflow, so blood can only flow in one direction through the heart.
